issues.item: Triggers: Animal Phobia: Talks or photos about snakes
issues.explanation: The snake-related trigger is hard to link coherently to the rest of this sexual-assault profile. Other triggers and strategies center on emergency/police/location cues, while no threat, appraisal, or memory content connects to animals or snakes. This makes that item look clinically disconnected rather than merely unusual.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Compulsive Cleaning: I clean or organise things repeatedly to feel in control
issues.explanation: Compulsive cleaning can occur after sexual assault, but in this profile it is not supported by the other selected items or the formulation. The active pattern strongly links triggers, threat, and negative appraisals to maladaptive strategies, yet the listed triggers/threats/appraisals point to hypervigilance, emergency/uniform cues, and situational avoidance rather than contamination, dirtiness, or washing/control themes. As selected here, the cleaning item appears insufficiently connected to the rest of the profile.

vignette:
Nader was 54, a single software engineer who had spent most of his adult life in the United States keeping his personal life carefully private, and that privacy had become more rigid since the assault. The event had happened years earlier after a late evening work function, when he had accepted a ride home from a man he knew only through colleagues. What began as ordinary conversation in the car turned suddenly coercive once they were alone; Nader described freezing, feeling overpowered, and afterward carrying a shame that made him question his own judgment more than the man's brutality. Even now, he spoke of the assault as deeply unfair, something that had happened to him and then been allowed to stand without any meaningful reckoning. He returned again and again to the thought that he had somehow invited it by the way he acted that night, and he feared that something in him had been permanently altered, that he would never feel normal emotions again.

In the months that followed, sounds and situations that resembled that night began to seize him. Sirens would cut through the street outside his apartment, and the sharp rise and fall of ambulances could pull him back into the same nauseated alertness he had felt when he was trying to get home and away from his assailant. Being alone with men, especially unfamiliar men, became intolerable; if he found himself in an elevator with a male coworker or cornered in a narrow corridor at work, his body reacted before he could reason with it. He started to avoid military and police uniforms, and even the sight of a weapon on someone's belt made him tense and look away. Going to the place where the event happened, or even driving past the street near it, became nearly impossible. Because those cues could appear without warning, his world shrank to a few places he considered safe, and he arranged his routines around staying inside them.

Nader came to believe that the danger was not only in those obvious reminders but in his own mind, which seemed to misread ordinary life as threat. He often reacted as if he were in danger even when nothing was actually wrong, and that constant sense of alarm kept him scanning his surroundings for signs of danger wherever he went. The more he scanned, the more proof he seemed to find that he was not safe, and the more he searched for exits, suspicious faces, or the glint of authority uniforms, the more certain he became that the world could turn on him without warning. That heightened vigilance fed his avoidance: he skipped client meetings if he knew security staff would be present, took longer routes to work to bypass the old neighborhood, and sat near exits in restaurants he otherwise liked. At the same time, the more he narrowed his life to those limited safe zones, the less he could test whether his fear was justified, and the stronger the feeling became that danger could be anywhere outside them.

His appraisals kept hardening around that shrinking life. The injustice of what had happened to him felt unbearable, particularly because he believed nothing had been done about it, and that sense of unresolved wrong sharpened his resentment each time he had to change his own behavior to avoid reminders. He blamed himself for the assault, revisiting his decision to accept the ride and the way he had spoken that night, and this self-blame made his avoidance feel necessary, almost deserved. Yet the same avoidance also became evidence to him that he had changed in a worse way than he wanted to admit: each cancelled errand, each refusal to be around uniforms or authority figures, seemed to confirm his fear that he could no longer feel like himself. The less he allowed himself to encounter the world, the more he distrusted his own reactions, and the more he felt that even ordinary moments might tip into threat.

At work, this had become visible in small but consequential ways. As a software engineer, he could still code alone, but he avoided the office on days when emergency vehicles were parked outside or when police were visible near the building, and he turned down social lunches if men he did not know would be present. Colleagues noticed his guardedness, though he rarely explained it. By the time he sought help, he was exhausted by the vigilance, the restricted routine, and the sense that his life had become organized around preventing panic rather than living it. What finally brought Nader in was the fear that the circle was closing further: that one more siren, one more uniform, one more accidental proximity to a man would send him back into the same dread. He wanted relief, but more than that, he wanted to know whether he could ever feel safe enough to move through the world again without constantly bracing for the worst.
